name: Cat Emotion Classification with ConvNeXt-Large
title: Iterating from 26% to High Accuracy: Cat Emotion Classification with ConvNeXt-Large
description: How I evolved a cat mood classifier from a struggling 26% baseline custom CNN into a fine-tuned ConvNeXt-Large pipeline using modern training techniques.
body:
Classifying feline emotions from web images sounds straightforward until you start looking at the data. Unlike human face datasets where landmarks are obvious, cat mood signals are subtle — a slight drop in the ear, a slight squint, or tense whiskers. Simple architectures tend to fail fast because they end up memorizing background textures instead of learning facial geometry.

When I first started testing on the Roboflow Cat Emotions dataset, I threw a small custom CNN with residual connections at the problem. It plateaued at a painful ~26% validation accuracy. It was clear the model lacked both capacity and pre-trained visual primitives. Upgrading to a standard pre-trained ResNet-50 and unfreezing all layers jumped performance straight to ~60%, proving that transfer learning was non-negotiable here.

To push things further, I switched the backbone to ConvNeXt-Large. But switching the architecture was only half the battle. What actually closed the generalization gap was dialing in the training stack.

I added `TrivialAugmentWide` for parameter-free data augmentation, which stopped the model from over-indexing on specific lighting conditions. Pairing AdamW with a cosine annealing schedule let the learning rate settle smoothly into local minima, while label smoothing (0.1) kept cross-entropy loss from making the predictions over-confident. Finally, running with Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) made it possible to train a backbone this size on an 8GB VRAM GPU without spilling memory, while gradient clipping kept training stable.

Combined, these adjustments transformed the project from an overfitted experiment into a usable model that accurately classifies emotions on unfamiliar cat photos instead of just memorizing the training set.

name: Conway Invaders: Building Space Invaders with Cellular Automata
title: Conway Invaders: Replacing Scripted Space Invaders with Cellular Automata
description: A Python & Pygame port and expansion of Conway Invaders, replacing standard enemy sprites with self-evolving cell grids and a dynamic, regenerating boss.
body:
Inspired by the classic C++/OpenGL project, I wanted to build a Python and Pygame port of Conway Invaders — an arcade shooter where the enemy fleet isn't made of pre-scripted sprites, but living patterns governed by John Conway's Game of Life.

The core loop shifts the feel of traditional Space Invaders. Every enemy wave evolves generation-by-generation in real time according to standard B3/S23 Conway rules. When you fire at an invader, your shots don't just reduce a health bar; they directly flip active cells to inactive. A single hit can disrupt an enemy cluster, causing it to decay into static blocks, collapse, or unpredictably split into moving gliders.

The centerpiece of the implementation is the dynamic boss fight. Instead of giving the boss a standard numerical HP bar, its health is tied directly to its live active cell count. If you don't sustain continuous damage, the pattern's cellular rules allow it to naturally regenerate lost sections during the fight.

To keep gameplay responsive, I included a 5-shot spread weapon mapped to the `X` key, specifically meant for tearing wide gaps in dense cellular formations before they expand toward your ship. Once the main campaign is cleared, the game opens up post-game modes, including a boss reset challenge and an endless sandbox mode for experimenting with rule interactions. The result is a shooter where you're constantly trying to contain or collapse living grid patterns that evolve under fire.

name: Multi-Architecture Autoencoders for Geological Anomaly Detection
title: Multi-Architecture Autoencoders for Geological Anomaly Detection
description: An end-to-end PyTorch framework running 10+ Autoencoder architectures to detect high-probability mineral deposit zones evaluated against real mine location shapefiles.
body:
In mineral exploration, spotting high-probability targets like Gold Porphyry from geochemical and geophysical survey maps is essentially an unsupervised anomaly problem. Most of a survey area consists of ordinary background rock, while the valuable mineral deposits appear as tiny, localized structural or compositional anomalies.

Instead of picking a single autoencoder design and hoping for the best, I built an end-to-end deep learning framework in PyTorch that trains 10+ autoencoder architectures in sequence, outputs normalized TIFF anomaly heatmaps, and automatically ranks their performance.

The framework covers a broad spectrum of models. On the baseline side, it evaluates standard, Convolutional (CAE), and ResNet-CAE architectures for spatial feature extraction. For probabilistic modeling, it runs Variational Autoencoders (VAE) and Beta-VAEs. To handle noise and perceptual consistency, it incorporates SSIM, Denoising, Masked, Contractive, and Sparse Autoencoders.

```bash
# Train all 10+ models and dump output TIFF heatmaps
python run_pipeline.py

# Benchmark heatmaps against known ground-truth mine shapefiles (.shp)
python evaluate_results.py
```

To figure out which architecture actually provides value on the ground, `evaluate_results.py` overlays generated heatmaps with shapefiles (`.shp`) of known deposit locations to compute AUC-ROC scores. This converts raw reconstruction errors into an objective ranking chart, giving geologists a clear, data-driven way to see which models best isolate real mineral targets and shortlist which core sections are worth sending to the lab.

name: Building a Local-First App with Tauri, SQLite WASM (OPFS), and Cloudflare KV
title: Building a Local-First App with Tauri, SQLite WASM (OPFS), and Encrypted Cloudflare KV Sync
description: How I turned a Tauri + SQLite desktop app into an offline-first React PWA at workstation.parsany.com using SQLite WASM in OPFS, plus an open-source Cloudflare Worker + KV sync backend (workstation-KV).
body: > **Try it live:** [workstation.parsany.com](https://workstation.parsany.com) runs 100% locally in your browser with offline PWA support. Want cross-device sync on your own free Cloudflare account? Deploy [github.com/parsany/workstation-KV](https://github.com/parsany/workstation-KV). Coming from my [Planner CLI](https://github.com/payrim/study_planner) and its Qt desktop variant, I originally built **Workstation** as a Tauri desktop app for my daily workflow — tasks, schedule capacity, `[[wikilink]]` notes with KaTeX math, pace tracking, and finances, all stored in a single local SQLite file. ![Workstation Desktop Knowledge view](/content/posts/workstation/desktop-knowledge.webp) After using it on Linux for a while, I wanted the exact same workspace on my phone and in any browser without maintaining two separate codebases or paying to host a central database. Because every query in the desktop app already went through one `SqlExecutor` interface, I split the repo into a TypeScript monorepo (`packages/core`, `packages/platform`, `apps/desktop`, `apps/web`). Roughly **85% of the code stays shared** in `@workstation/core` — all the domain logic, adaptive capacity planner, 22-table SQLite migrations (`v1`–`v10`), repositories, and React context. `@workstation/platform` just swaps `@tauri-apps/plugin-sql` on Desktop for `@sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm` in the browser, while `apps/desktop` and `apps/web` act as thin shells on top. ![Workstation Desktop Schedule & Time Ledger](/content/posts/workstation/desktop-schedule.webp) ## Running Real SQLite in the Browser (OPFS + WASM) The web version at [workstation.parsany.com](https://workstation.parsany.com) doesn't talk to a backend database API. It's an installable PWA (`vite-plugin-pwa`) running `@sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm` inside a dedicated Web Worker backed by the browser's Origin Private File System (**OPFS**), so every visitor gets their own isolated `workstation.db` file with zero latency and full offline support. Wiring up the web port did hit a few real-world gotchas. Without `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` in Cloudflare Pages `_headers`, `sqlite-wasm` silently falls back to `:memory:` and wipes your data on refresh. Pulling a backup on the web also froze the UI at first because every individual `INSERT` triggered its own OPFS flush, which went away as soon as I wrapped the import loop in `BEGIN TRANSACTION` / `COMMIT`. On the bundle side, the production web build comes out to **~348 KB gzipped JS** plus **~396 KB gzipped `sqlite3.wasm`** (**2.26 MB** total across 10 Workbox precached assets), so it launches offline cleanly. ![Workstation Web PWA Dashboard](/content/posts/workstation/web-dashboard.webp) ## Zero-Knowledge Sync Without Hosting Anyone's Data (`workstation-KV`) To sync between desktop and phone, I didn't want OAuth, user tables, or a central database holding people's private notes and finances. Instead, I wrote a small standalone Cloudflare Worker called [workstation-KV](https://github.com/parsany/workstation-KV) (**1.65 KB gzipped**, zero npm runtime dependencies) that anyone can deploy to their own free Cloudflare account. When you press **Sync** in Workstation: 1. **Local AES-256-GCM encryption**: Your device exports the 22 SQLite tables to JSON, derives an encryption key from your password via PBKDF2 (`100,000` iterations), and encrypts the payload *before* it leaves your device. 2. **Server-side Worker auth**: Your Worker checks `X-Sync-User` and `X-Sync-Pass` against Cloudflare Worker Secrets (`SYNC_USERNAME` and salted `PBKDF2-SHA256` `SYNC_PASSWORD_HASH`) using constant-time comparison. Nothing secret is ever hardcoded in the static React bundle. 3. **Timestamp check**: Before pushing or pulling, the client compares `exportedAt` metadata via `GET /sync/meta` so a stale device never blindly overwrites newer edits. ```bash npx wrangler kv namespace create SYNC_KV node scripts/hash-password.mjs "YOUR_STRONG_PASSWORD" npx wrangler secret put SYNC_USERNAME npx wrangler secret put SYNC_PASSWORD_HASH npx wrangler deploy ``` ## Engineering Trade-Offs & Free-Tier Numbers I went with full-snapshot JSON sync over CRDTs or per-row op-logs because it's simple, transactional, and fits one person switching between desktop and phone sequentially — CRDTs only become worth the complexity for real-time multi-user editing. Same with Cloudflare KV vs. D1: KV is eventually consistent (totally fine for a manual Sync button) and stores one encrypted blob per user (`workspace:`), whereas D1 would make sense if I ever turned this into a multi-user hosted SaaS. Keeping `workstation-KV` open source means anyone can run their own Worker on Cloudflare's free tier (**100,000 reads/day**, **1,000 writes/day**, **1 GB storage**, **25 MiB per key**) at **$0/month**, and I never hold anyone else's data. ## Sync Safety, Conflicts & Recovery Snapshot sync has clear boundaries, so it helps to be explicit about how conflicts and recovery work. Each device stores `lastSyncedRemoteExportedAt` locally; when you hit **Sync Now**, it checks `GET /sync/meta` first and automatically pushes or pulls if only one side changed. If *both* the local database and the cloud snapshot changed since the last sync, it stops and asks you to choose **Push Local** or **Pull Cloud** instead of silently overwriting anything. Because `AES-256-GCM` encryption happens locally with your password, there is no server-side password reset — if you forget it, the cloud ciphertext can't be decrypted, though your local SQLite file on Desktop or OPFS stays untouched and you can push a fresh snapshot with a new password. Both Desktop and Web also have standalone **Export JSON / Restore JSON** backups that work offline without Cloudflare, and if a device is ever lost, rotating `SYNC_USERNAME` and `SYNC_PASSWORD_HASH` on your Worker immediately revokes its access. ![Workstation Web PWA Analytics and Backups](/content/posts/workstation/web-analytics.webp) ## Getting Started You can try the web/mobile PWA right away at [workstation.parsany.com](https://workstation.parsany.com) (installable from Chrome or Safari, with everything stored in your browser's OPFS SQLite). If you want the desktop app or want to run the monorepo locally (Node 20+, `pnpm`, and Rust/Tauri CLI for desktop builds), grab the source at [github.com/parsany/Workstation](https://github.com/parsany/Workstation) (private for now), and deploy [github.com/parsany/workstation-KV](https://github.com/parsany/workstation-KV) to your own Cloudflare account if you want cross-device sync.
